cards.title: Spanners matching Thorup–Zwick emulator tradeoffs
cards.formal:
For every fixed integer \(k\ge1\), do there exist constants \(C_{k},D_{k}>0\) such that every finite simple undirected unweighted graph \(G=(V,E)\), with \(n=|V|\ge1\), has a spanning subgraph \(H=(V,E_{H})\), \(E_{H}\subseteq E\), satisfying
\[
|E_{H}|\le C_{k}n^{\,1+1/(2^{k+1}-1)}
\]
and, simultaneously for all distinct vertices \(u,v\) in the same connected component of \(G\),
\[
d_{H}(u,v)\le d_{G}(u,v)+D_{k}\,d_{G}(u,v)^{\,1-1/k}?
\]
The constants may depend on \(k\), but not on the graph, its size or the vertex pair. This is the fixed-\(k\) size and distance-error tradeoff achieved by Thorup–Zwick emulators, now required of an actual subgraph.
cards.why: Spanners retain real routes in the original network, while emulators can encode long routes as weighted shortcuts. Matching their size/error tradeoffs would establish that this structural restriction costs only constant factors at every fixed level of sublinear distance accuracy. The later almost-matching theorem makes the exact remaining loss especially concrete.

cards.definitions:
The distance \(d_{G}(u,v)\) is the number of edges on a shortest path in \(G\); it is \(+\infty\) if there is no path. A spanning subgraph keeps every vertex and may remove edges, but all retained edges still have unit length. It cannot insert shortcut edges or change weights. Consequently, \(d_{H}(u,v)\ge d_{G}(u,v)\) automatically.

The inequality for finite distances requires \(H\) to connect every pair originally connected in \(G\). Vertices in different components remain disconnected because \(H\subseteq G\). Equal vertices have distance zero in both graphs and need no separate distortion inequality. For distinct connected vertices, \(d_{G}(u,v)\ge1\), so the power is defined even at \(k=1\), where it equals 1.

There is one subgraph \(H\) for the entire graph and fixed \(k\). It must satisfy the bound for every distance scale and every pair simultaneously. The quantifier order is
\[
\forall k\ge1\ \exists C_{k},D_{k}>0\ \forall G\ \exists H\ \forall u,v.
\]
The size bound has no hidden logarithmic factor in \(n\), no \(n^{\delta}\) loss for positive \(\delta\), and no additional accuracy parameter affecting the selected subgraph. Dependence on a growing \(k=k(n)\) is not requested.

For \(k>1\), the allowed additive error is sublinear in the distance because \(d^{1-1/k}/d=d^{-1/k}\) tends to zero. It need not be a constant independent of distance. For example, \(k=2\) asks for \(O(n^{8/7})\) edges with additive error \(O(\sqrt d)\). The \(k=1\) case asks for \(O(n^{4/3})\) edges and constant additive error.

An emulator is a weighted graph on the same vertex set that may contain edges absent from \(G\). A shortcut between \(u,v\) can receive weight \(d_{G}(u,v)\), preserving the prohibition on underestimating original distances. A spanner must instead use only original edges. Replacing shortcuts by their full original paths can increase the number of retained edges and does not automatically preserve the size bound.

The main assertion is existential: it asks for the same structural tradeoff, not a prescribed transformation of a supplied emulator or a specified construction running time. A construction establishing these bounds qualifies. This follows the size/stretch question in the source; bounds on construction time are separate from this target.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed existence assertion for every fixed integer \(k\), or refute it by showing that for some fixed \(k\) no constants \(C_{k},D_{k}\) work for all graphs. A counterexample to one proposed construction is insufficient. A family with the stated edge exponent plus any fixed positive slack, or different spanners for different accuracy parameters, does not establish the exact target.

context_blocks.title: The emulator hierarchy supplies the benchmark
context_blocks.text: Thorup and Zwick’s Theorem 4.1 gives emulators with the required sublinear distance error and \(O(k n^{1+1/(2^{k+1}-1)})\) edges after shifting their parameter by one. For fixed \(k\), the factor \(k\) is absorbed into the size constant. The tutorial asks whether actual subgraphs can match this tradeoff.

context_blocks.title: All accuracy scales belong to one graph
context_blocks.text: The 2018 hierarchy paper emphasizes that a sublinear-error spanner has corresponding near-additive guarantees for all accuracy choices on the same graph. A construction whose size or chosen edge set depends on a separately supplied \(\varepsilon\) does not automatically give this simultaneous property.

context_blocks.title: The later spanner construction comes arbitrarily close in the exponent
context_blocks.text: Tan and Zhang’s Theorem 1.1 proves that for every fixed \(k\ge2\) and \(\delta>0\), there is a spanner with \(O(n^{1+(1+\delta)/(2^{k+1}-1)})\) edges and error \(C(k,\delta)d^{1-1/k}\). This is a major improvement over the bounds recorded by the tutorial, but still has positive exponent slack.

context_blocks.title: The endpoint does not follow by sending the slack to zero
context_blocks.text: The later theorem permits its constants to depend on \(\delta\). Its Section 4 bound explicitly allows the stretch coefficient to grow as \(\delta\) decreases. Thus taking smaller fixed slack, or choosing slack as a function of \(n\), does not supply a fixed \(D_{k}\) and the exact required edge bound.

context_blocks.title: The first level is already known
context_blocks.text: The known additive-six spanner on \(O(n^{4/3})\) edges settles \(k=1\). The unresolved hierarchy begins with the square-root distance error at \(k=2\) and continues through the higher fixed levels.

cards.context:
Thorup and Zwick’s Theorem 4.1 gives emulators with the required sublinear distance error and \(O(k n^{1+1/(2^{k+1}-1)})\) edges after shifting their parameter by one. For fixed \(k\), the factor \(k\) is absorbed into the size constant. The tutorial asks whether actual subgraphs can match this tradeoff.

The 2018 hierarchy paper emphasizes that a sublinear-error spanner has corresponding near-additive guarantees for all accuracy choices on the same graph. A construction whose size or chosen edge set depends on a separately supplied \(\varepsilon\) does not automatically give this simultaneous property.

Tan and Zhang’s Theorem 1.1 proves that for every fixed \(k\ge2\) and \(\delta>0\), there is a spanner with \(O(n^{1+(1+\delta)/(2^{k+1}-1)})\) edges and error \(C(k,\delta)d^{1-1/k}\). This is a major improvement over the bounds recorded by the tutorial, but still has positive exponent slack.

The later theorem permits its constants to depend on \(\delta\). Its Section 4 bound explicitly allows the stretch coefficient to grow as \(\delta\) decreases. Thus taking smaller fixed slack, or choosing slack as a function of \(n\), does not supply a fixed \(D_{k}\) and the exact required edge bound.

The known additive-six spanner on \(O(n^{4/3})\) edges settles \(k=1\). The unresolved hierarchy begins with the square-root distance error at \(k=2\) and continues through the higher fixed levels.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
